speech.text: Here are three animals that handle death just like humans do. First up, dolphins. For them, death means sinking. So, when a calf passes away, the mother will desperately try to push its body to the surface using her head or back. She keeps doing this until she's exhausted, often getting sunburned from staying above water for so long. Other dolphins will form a protective circle around the grieving mom to keep sharks away. Every dolphin has a unique signature whistle, kind of like a name. When one dies, the others will keep making that sound, as if they're calling out the name of the one they lost. Next, elephants. Besides humans, they are the only ones who can recognize the bones of their own kind. When an elephant dies, the whole herd stands guard over the body for days. They lower their ears, stay completely silent, and some even shed tears in grief. They eventually cover the body with leaves and dirt, a primitive form of burial. They even return to the site years later to gently touch the bones, remembering their lost friend. And what about crows? When a crow finds a dead body, it lets out a specific alarm call. Within minutes, hundreds will gather around. After a burst of loud calling, the whole flock goes into a strange silence for about 30 minutes. Scientists believe they're actually studying how it died, so they can avoid that danger zone in the future.
